correctness.rationale: For \(\Omega(n)\le4\), the five exponent partitions give sharp prime-minimized abundancy upper bounds, the largest being \(14/5<3\), so no triperfect number occurs. If \(\Omega(n)=5\), an odd triperfect number is impossible because the modern stronger theorem on odd triperfect numbers gives at least twelve distinct prime factors; independently, the parity criterion also forces an odd triperfect integer to be a square, contradicting odd \(\Omega\). Writing \(n=2^a m\), the cases \(a=5,4,3,2,1\) close exactly as in the submitted proof. Fresh exact-rational reconstruction reproduced the critical maxima, the unique \(a=3\) solution \((q,r)=(3,5)\), and no \(a=2\) squarefree-three-prime solution. Cohen's Theorem 4 independently confirms that a triperfect integer divisible by \(2^2\cdot3\cdot5\) is \(120\).
correctness.risk: The proof classifies only the minimal multiplicity layer; it does not classify triperfect numbers with larger \(\Omega\).

final_claim: Every triperfect integer \(n\), meaning \(\sigma(n)=3n\), satisfies \(\Omega(n)\ge5\); moreover \(\Omega(n)=5\) holds exactly for \(n=120=2^3\cdot3\cdot5\).
